messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Parole Officer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Kwame's Story

Kwame was thirty-four when he came to the clinic, referred by his supervisor at the Department of Corrections after he'd requested a leave of absence. He'd been a parole officer for eight years, known for his thoroughness and his ability to build rapport with clients—men and women cycling back into the community after incarceration. That reputation had begun to fracture in the months since March, when his partner of three years, Devon, had put him in the hospital.

The night itself had started as an argument about money, about Kwame working late again, about attention withheld. Devon had been drinking. What Kwame remembered most vividly now was not the sequence of blows but the moment after—lying on the kitchen tile, the taste of blood and salt thick in his mouth, Devon's voice above him, low and certain, saying things Kwame could no longer quite articulate but could still hear perfectly when his mind returned to that kitchen. The ambulance had smelled of bleach and something chemical, a hospital smell that had filled his nostrils as the paramedics worked. That smell had stayed with him. Now, whenever he caught it—in a clinic waiting room, in the hallway outside a courthouse where he sometimes had to testify—his body went rigid. His chest would tighten. He would feel, for a moment, like he was back on that tile.

In the weeks after, Kwama had tried to move forward. He'd left Devon, found a new apartment, returned to work. But his body had not returned with him. He described it as being constantly braced, as though his muscles were waiting for impact that might come at any moment. Walking through the parole office, he found himself tracking the movements of his male colleagues—noting where they stood, whether they were looking at him, calculating angles and exits. When a colleague named Marcus had complimented his shirt one morning, something in the way Marcus's eyes had lingered had sent a spike of fear through Kwame that he couldn't quite justify but couldn't shake either. He'd begun avoiding the break room when men were there. He'd stopped making eye contact during staff meetings, keeping his gaze fixed on his notes or his hands.

The avoidance had spread quietly. When his supervisor suggested they grab lunch to discuss his workload, Kwame had found reasons to decline—first once, then repeatedly. Conflict, even the mild kind that lived in a conversation about performance metrics, felt dangerous. His body would anticipate harm before his mind could catch up. So he said yes to everything, agreed to everything, and felt his resentment calcify. When his sister called with good news—she was getting married—Kwame had felt something close to panic. Happiness felt like a trap, like letting his guard down, like inviting disaster. He'd been short with her. He'd pushed the joy away because joy meant softness, and softness meant vulnerability.

By September, six months after the hospital, Kwame was isolated in ways he couldn't quite explain to anyone who asked. He'd stopped seeing friends. He'd become hypervigilant at work in a way that was beginning to show—his supervisor had noted that he seemed "on edge," that his casework was thorough but increasingly withdrawn. When a client had looked at him a certain way during an intake—a lingering gaze that might have meant nothing—Kwame had felt objectified, seen in a way that made his skin crawl. He'd finished that appointment early.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a moment of clarity that had felt like drowning. He'd been sitting in his apartment, alone, and realized he couldn't remember the last time he'd felt safe. More than that: he'd begun to wonder, in the dark hours, whether the effort of staying vigilant, of staying separate, of staying alive in this fractured way, was worth the cost. He'd called his sister back. He'd told her he needed help. Now, sitting across from the therapist, Kwame was afraid of two things equally: that he would be asked to relive what happened, and that he would be told that his life—this small, defended, isolated life he'd built—was all he had left.
